title: Low-budget online marketing: use inventory limits, quit bad channels fast, fix the website first
summary: Jason Cohen explains how cash-strapped startups should choose among marketing channels. Decide whether to optimize a channel by how much untapped inventory remains, abandon channels that fail out of the gate, optimize the website before any single campaign, and chase only large effects because small-sample data is mostly noise.

principles.text: Decide whether to optimize a channel by remaining inventory; if you can get 2x or more, go get it.
principles.quote: If you think there's 2x or more inventory you could go get, I say go get it.

principles.text: When a channel nears its inventory limit, stop optimizing it and find new campaigns that can double the business.
principles.quote: Once you approach inventory limits, you need to find other campaigns which can [double your business]

principles.text: Don't give a failing new channel the benefit of the doubt; campaigns that start bad tend to stay bad, so cut out early.
principles.quote: the ones that were bad out of the gate tended to stay bad.

principles.text: Optimize the website before individual campaigns, since every campaign flows through it and gains compound.
principles.quote: Optimizations you do on your website are more valuable than those you do on individual marketing campaigns. The reason is obvious in retrospect: all marketing campaigns lead there!

principles.text: When small, only pursue large effects: little data is statistically significant, so small gains are indistinguishable from noise.
principles.quote: When you're small, almost no data you have is statistically significant.  Therefore, most variation you see is due to random fluctuations, not real results

principles.text: With big budgets, try many channels fast and burn cash for learning; with low budgets, don't copy that approach.
